title: Lesson 0 · Collaboration, Honor Code, and AI
text: Lesson 0 · Collaboration, Honor Code, and AI The line the course draws: talking is encouraged, code is not shared . "You are encouraged to discuss the homework and lab assignments with each other, but you may not view or copy another student's code." Honor code Discuss problems and teach each other — the slides call this "one of the most effective ways to learn." No viewing or copying another student's code. No sharing solutions. No posting assignments on GitHub or other public websites. Note for your own repos. That last rule covers public GitHub repositories — so keep COMP 211 lab code out of any public repo, including a personal portfolio or a study-guide repo like this one. Course notes are fine; assignment code is not. AI usage What you can't do Copy and paste any part of an assignment into an AI tool — that includes code, prompts, and the full problem text. What you can do Use AI like you would use a TA : ask questions, get clarification, strengthen your understanding. The course's own framing: "AI is most useful when it helps you think through a problem, not when it replaces your work." The stated reason is not suspicion — it is that "the skills you build are the same skills you'll rely on in your job." How to ask a good question The slides give three model questions. Notice the shape: each one states what you already understand and exactly where you are stuck . "Can you explain the purpose of dynamic memory allocation? I understand that malloc, realloc, and calloc allocate memory on the heap, but I'm not sure why that's useful." "What's the difference between strncpy and strlcpy? I think one always includes a null terminator, but I cannot remember which one. Is one of them considered safer?" "Can you help me understand this error message? I know the issue is on line 21. What are some common causes of this type of error, and what should I check?" Scenario You are stuck on a lab. Which of these is allowed under the course AI policy? Paste the lab's problem statement into a chatbot and ask how to approach it Paste your buggy lab function in and ask it to fix the bug Ask "what are common causes of a segmentation fault when indexing an array?" in your own words Ask a classmate to send you their working version to compare against Only the third. It contains no assignment text and no code — it is a conceptual question you could equally ask a TA. Options 0 and 1 both paste assignment material (problem text counts, not just code), and option 4 is viewing another student's code.

title: Lesson 0 · Binary and Number Bases
text: Lesson 0 · Binary and Number Bases A base is the number of different digits a system can use to represent numbers. Decimal is base-10 (digits 0–9). Binary is base-2 (digits 0 and 1). Computers use binary because the building block of a computer is a transistor — a switch that is either off (0) or on (1). Bits Each digit of a binary number is a bit . One bit represents two values; the number of values doubles with every bit you add. Bits Distinct values Range 1 2 1 = 2 0–1 2 2 2 = 4 0–3 3 2 3 = 8 0–7 4 2 4 = 16 0–15 8 (one byte) 2 8 = 256 0–255 Memorize the pattern, not the table: n bits give 2 n values, spanning 0 through 2 n −1. That "minus one" is the source of an enormous number of bugs. The 0b prefix When you write a binary number, you must mark it as binary by prepending 0b . Why this matters. Write 10 and everyone reads ten . Write 0b10 and it is unambiguously two . The slides call this out explicitly: without the 0b , "we would assume that it is the decimal number ten!" Decimal Binary (2 bits) Binary (3 bits) Binary (4 bits) 0 0b00 0b000 0b0000 1 0b01 0b001 0b0001 2 0b10 0b010 0b0010 3 0b11 0b011 0b0011 4 — 0b100 0b0100 7 — 0b111 0b0111 15 — — 0b1111 Notice what happens when you widen the field: the values 0–3 just gain leading zeros. Leading zeros never change the value — they only change how many bits you are using. Converting Binary → decimal: add up the place values Each position is a power of two, counting from the right , starting at 2 0 . 0b 1 0 1 1 | | | | 8 4 2 1 <- place values 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11 Decimal → binary: greedy subtraction Take the largest power of two that fits, write a 1, subtract, repeat. 13: 8 fits -> 1, remainder 5 4 fits -> 1, remainder 1 2 no -> 0 1 fits -> 1, remainder 0 = 0b1101 Use the lab on the next tab to check yourself — click bits on and off and watch the decimal value follow.

title: Lesson 1 · Terminal, Shell, and CLI
text: Lesson 1 · Terminal, Shell, and CLI Three words that get used interchangeably and shouldn't be. CLI is the interaction style . Terminal is the app you type into . Shell is the program that actually understands and runs your commands . Term What it is Examples Command-line interface (CLI) A text-based way to interact with a system — a style , not a program Bash CLI, PowerShell CLI, Git's command-line usage Terminal The application/window that displays text, sends your keystrokes to a shell, and shows the shell's output Terminal.app (macOS), Windows Terminal, GNOME Terminal, iTerm2 Shell The command interpreter — the program that reads your command and executes it bash (this course), zsh, fish, sh, PowerShell, cmd.exe This course uses Bash , the default shell on Linux. When you open a terminal for the class it auto-launches bash and shows a shell prompt — the shell's way of saying "I'm ready for a command." The interaction loop prompt appears -> you type a command -> you press Enter ^ | | v +-------- computer responds with text ----+ That loop is the whole idea of a CLI. Contrast it with a GUI, where you click. Why the terminal is still here How we got here Era What changed Early computers (ENIAC, EDSAC) Batch processing — punched cards in, printout hours or days later. No interaction; one mistake meant re-running the entire job. Teletypes (TTYs) The first interactive text interface : type characters, get characters back, printed line by line on paper. CRTs (e.g. VT100) Cursor movement, overwriting text, screen-based editing, faster feedback. The word "terminal" stuck even though the technology changed. Late 1970s–80s Cheaper memory, better displays, the mouse → GUIs , and computers became usable by non-experts. Why it survived the GUI Scriptable — a command you can type is a command you can automate Remote-friendly — text travels well over a network Extremely powerful Servers frequently have no GUI at all The philosophical shift the slides highlight: computers went from "machines that run jobs" to "systems you work with" — which is what made interactive programming, real-time debugging, exploratory computing, networking, and remote login possible. Multiple choice You open Terminal.app on a Mac and type ls . Which component actually interprets and executes that command? Terminal.app The CLI The shell (bash or zsh) The operating system kernel, directly The shell is the command interpreter. Terminal.app only displays text and forwards your keystrokes; "CLI" names the interaction style, not a program. (The shell does ask the kernel to do the work, but it is the shell that parses and runs the command.) True / False "Terminal" and "shell" are two names for the same program. True False Different layers. You can run different shells inside the same terminal (bash, zsh, fish), and the same shell inside different terminals. The terminal is the window; the shell is the interpreter.

title: Lesson 6 · Decimal & Binary Notation
text: Lesson 6 · Decimal & Binary Notation Both decimal and binary are positional number systems: the value of a digit depends on where it sits, not just what symbol it is. In decimal, each position is a power of 10 ; in binary, each position is a power of 2 . Decimal, recapped Take 5072. Each digit is multiplied by the power of 10 for its position, and the results are summed: 5072 = (5 × 10 3 ) + (0 × 10 2 ) + (7 × 10 1 ) + (2 × 10 0 ) = 5000 + 0 + 70 + 2 If you don't see a prefix on a number at all, the default interpretation is decimal — that's the "unmarked" base. Binary: the same idea, base 2 Binary digits are called bits , and each position is a power of 2 instead of 10. Bits are numbered starting from the rightmost bit, which is bit 0 (written d 0 ) — also called the least significant bit (LSB) . For an n -bit number, the leftmost bit is bit n−1 , the most significant bit (MSB) . 1011 2 = (1 × 2 3 ) + (0 × 2 2 ) + (1 × 2 1 ) + (1 × 2 0 ) = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11 (decimal) Binary is written two ways: prefixed with 0b (e.g. 0b1001 ) or subscripted with a 2 (e.g. 1001 2 ). Both mean exactly the same thing. Grouping bits for readability Long strings of bits are hard to read, so binary is conventionally grouped in 4s : Context Separator Example Handwritten space 0b1010 1111 0101 Typed / in code underscore 0b1010_1111_0101 If the total number of bits doesn't divide evenly into groups of 4, build the groups from the right , letting the leftmost group be short: 0b10_1010_0011 (a leading group of just 2 bits, then two full groups of 4). The 0–15 binary reference table You are expected to know this table by heart — it's the foundation for every conversion and every hex digit that follows. Decimal Binary Decimal Binary 0 0000 8 1000 1 0001 9 1001 2 0010 10 1010 3 0011 11 1011 4 0100 12 1100 5 0101 13 1101 6 0110 14 1110 7 0111 15 1111 What "unsigned" means, and why 9+1 needs a new digit A number is unsigned when it can only represent zero or positive values — never negative. Plain binary, as introduced so far, is unsigned. In decimal, a single digit can only store the values 0–9. Add 1 to 9 and there is no single digit left to represent "10" — you must carry into a new, more-significant digit. Binary works identically: a single bit can only store 0 or 1. Add 1 to a bit that is already 1, and it overflows into the next bit position, exactly the way decimal digits overflow into the next column. Multiple choice In the binary number 10110 , which bit is bit 0? The leftmost bit The middle bit The rightmost bit Whichever bit is a 1 Bits are numbered starting from the rightmost bit as bit 0 (the least significant bit). The leftmost bit of an n -bit number is bit n−1, the most significant bit. True / False An unsigned number can represent zero, but never a negative value. True False True — "unsigned" means the encoding is restricted to zero and positive values.

title: Lesson 6 · Binary <-> Decimal Conversion
text: Lesson 6 · Binary <-> Decimal Conversion Binary → decimal Multiply each bit by its power of 2, and sum the results: 1011 2 = (1×2 3 ) + (0×2 2 ) + (1×2 1 ) + (1×2 0 ) = 8+0+2+1 = 11 Decimal → binary: the subtraction algorithm The textbook's algorithm, repeated until the remainder hits 0: Find the largest power of 2 that is ≤ the current number. Place a 1 in that bit position of the answer. Subtract that power of 2 from the current number. Repeat with the remainder, until it reaches 0. Worked example: 114 → binary 114 - 64 = 50 bit set: 64 (2 6 ) 50 - 32 = 18 bit set: 32 (2 5 ) 18 - 16 = 2 bit set: 16 (2 4 ) 2 - 2 = 0 bit set: 2 (2 1 ) 2 6 2 5 2 4 2 3 2 2 2 1 2 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 = 0b1110010 Every power of 2 not used along the way gets a 0 in the answer — that's why bit positions 2 3 , 2 2 , and 2 0 are 0 above. Alternate mental-math approach: powers of 2 that add up Lecture also shows a quicker, informal shortcut for small numbers: think of the value as a sum of distinct powers of 2 you already recognize, then flip on those bits directly. This is not the primary algorithm above — it's a mental-math shortcut once you're comfortable with the powers of 2. 7 = 4 + 2 + 1 → 0b0111 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 → 0b1101 Multiple choice Converting decimal 114 to binary, after subtracting 64 you're left with 50. What's the next step? Immediately write down the answer Find the largest power of 2 ≤ 50, mark that bit, and subtract it Divide 50 by 2 and round Start over from 114 The algorithm repeats step 1–3 on the remainder each time: largest power of 2 ≤ 50 is 32, so you set that bit and subtract, leaving 18. Fill in the blank Convert 1011 2 to decimal (unsigned). Check (1×8)+(0×4)+(1×2)+(1×1) = 8+0+2+1 = 11.

title: Lesson 6 · Hexadecimal
text: Lesson 6 · Hexadecimal Hexadecimal is base 16 : sixteen digits, 0–9 then A–F standing in for 10–15. It's written with a 0x prefix ( 0x3A ) or subscripted with 16 ( 3A 16 ). Why bother, if we already have decimal and binary? Decimal doesn't align cleanly with powers of two, which makes it a poor fit for reasoning about fixed-size binary data — a 16-bit address, for instance, doesn't break into tidy decimal chunks. Hexadecimal is convenient for exactly that job: each hex digit maps cleanly onto exactly 4 bits , so a whole binary value collapses into a short, precise hex string. That's also why memory addresses are almost always displayed in hex — they're stored in binary, but hex is far more compact and human-readable than writing out the raw bits. Binary → hex Group the binary digits into groups of 4 , working from right to left . If the leftmost group is short, prepend leading zeros to complete it. Convert each group of 4 bits into its single hex digit. Worked example 0b111010 → 0b0011_1010 (leading zeros added to complete the left group) 0011 = 3 1010 = A → 0x3A Hex → binary Convert each hex digit to its 4-bit binary equivalent; leading zeros can optionally be dropped afterward. 0x3F54 → 0b0011_1111_0101_0100 (or, dropping the leading zeros: 0b11_1111_0101_0100) Full 0–15 reference table (decimal / binary / hex) Decimal Binary Hex Decimal Binary Hex 0 0000 0 8 1000 8 1 0001 1 9 1001 9 2 0010 2 10 1010 A 3 0011 3 11 1011 B 4 0100 4 12 1100 C 5 0101 5 13 1101 D 6 0110 6 14 1110 E 7 0111 7 15 1111 F Multiple choice Why is hexadecimal especially convenient for humans working with binary data? Each hex digit maps cleanly onto exactly 4 bits Hex numbers are always shorter than decimal numbers Computers only understand hex internally Hex avoids the need for negative numbers The 4-bit-per-digit mapping is exact and lossless, which is what makes hex a compact, readable stand-in for raw binary — especially for things like memory addresses. Fill in the blank Convert 0b111010 to hexadecimal. Check Pad to 0b0011_1010 → 0011=3, 1010=A → 0x3A .

title: Lesson 6 · Unsigned & the Problem of Negatives
text: Lesson 6 · Unsigned & the Problem of Negatives Plain binary as covered so far is unsigned : every bit pattern maps to zero or a positive value, and there is no way to write a negative number. That limitation is exactly what motivates signed encodings — schemes that carve out some bit patterns to represent negative values. A key framing detail for signed encodings: they typically split the available bit patterns roughly evenly — about half assigned to negative values, and about half to non-negative (zero and positive) values. It is not the case that vastly more patterns go to one side than the other. True / False Signed binary encodings typically assign far more bit patterns to positive values than to negative ones. True False False — the split is roughly even , about half negative and half non-negative.

title: Lesson 6 · One's Complement
text: Lesson 6 · One's Complement One's complement is a way to represent negative numbers in binary. Positive values are written exactly like unsigned binary, except they must begin with a leading 0 bit — even if the plain unsigned form wouldn't otherwise need one. Negative values are formed by taking the positive counterpart and flipping every bit (0s become 1s, 1s become 0s). Value Steps Result +5 unsigned 101, add leading 0 0b0101 −5 flip every bit of 0b0101 0b1010 −10 flip every bit of 0b0_1010 0b1_0101 −15 flip every bit of 0b0_1111 0b1_0000 Rule: in one's complement, every positive value has MSB 0 , and every negative value has MSB 1 . Check the leading bit and you know the sign immediately. Worked examples (slide style) Represent −5 in 7-bit one's complement Step 1: write +5 as unsigned in 7 bits → 0b0000101 . Step 2: flip every bit → 0b1111010 . Represent +4 in 6-bit one's complement It's positive, so no bit flip is needed — just write 4 in unsigned 6-bit form: 0b000100 . The shortcoming: two zeros One's complement has two distinct representations of zero: all zeros ( 000...0 ) and all ones ( 111...1 , which flips to "negative zero"). That wastes a bit pattern that could otherwise represent one additional, unique value. Multiple choice To write +4 in 6-bit one's complement, what do you do? Write 4 in unsigned 6-bit form, then flip every bit Just write 4 in unsigned 6-bit form — no flip, it's positive Flip only the MSB Add 1 to the unsigned form Positive values in one's complement are unsigned binary with a leading-0 sign bit guaranteed. The bit-flip step only applies when forming a negative value. Multiple choice What is the key shortcoming of one's complement? It can't represent negative numbers It requires more bits than unsigned binary Zero has two distinct representations, wasting a bit pattern The MSB doesn't indicate sign All-zeros and all-ones both mean "zero," which is one wasted pattern that two's complement later reclaims.

title: Lesson 6 · Two's Complement
text: Lesson 6 · Two's Complement Two's complement fixes one's complement's wasted double-zero: by reclaiming the extra all-ones pattern, an n -bit range gains exactly one more representable negative value at the low end. E.g. a range that maxed out at −3 in one's complement can now reach −4 in two's complement. Decimal → two's complement Find the one's complement representation. If the number is negative , add 1 to that one's complement result. (If positive, stop here — identical to one's complement, no further step.) Worked example: express −7 in 6-bit two's complement one's complement of +7: 0b000111 one's complement of -7 (flip): 0b111000 add 1 (because negative): 0b111001 Two's complement binary → decimal Check the MSB . If it's 0 , the number is positive — read it exactly like unsigned binary and stop. If the MSB is 1 , the number is negative. Flip every bit. Add 1 to the flipped result. The original value is the negative of that final result. Worked example: convert 0b1101 to decimal MSB is 1 -> negative flip bits: 0b0010 add 1: 0b0011 = 3 original value = -3 Key advantage: two's complement has only one representation of zero (all zeros) — no wasted pattern. And in both one's and two's complement, the MSB alone tells you the sign: 0 = positive, 1 = negative. Multiple choice What is two's complement's key advantage over one's complement? It uses fewer bits It has only one representation of zero Negative numbers don't need a sign bit Addition and subtraction use different rules Reclaiming the redundant all-ones "zero" gives two's complement a single zero representation and one extra negative value at the low end of the range. Fill in the blank Express -7 in 6-bit two's complement. Check One's complement of +7 is 000111; flip to get one's complement of -7: 111000; add 1: 111001 . Fill in the blank Convert two's-complement 0b1101 to decimal. Check MSB=1 (negative). Flip → 0010, add 1 → 0011 = 3, so the value is -3 .

It can represent zero or positive values, but not negative values It can represent any negative value only It has no fixed number of bits It is stored as a hexadecimal string Unsigned → zero and positive only. Because digits cannot store values larger than 9 Because 9 is an odd number Because decimal doesn't support addition Because 9 is the base of the system A single decimal digit is capped at 9; going past it forces a carry into a new, more-significant digit. (8×10 2 ) + (4×10 3 ) + (2×10 1 ) + (5×10 0 ) (8×10 3 ) + (4×10 2 ) + (2×10 1 ) + (5×10 0 ) (8×10 0 ) + (4×10 1 ) + (2×10 2 ) + (5×10 3 ) (8×10 4 ) + (4×10 3 ) + (2×10 2 ) + (5×10 1 ) Positions go from the left : thousands (10 3 ), hundreds (10 2 ), tens (10 1 ), ones (10 0 ) — matching option 1. Unsigned numbers cannot represent negative values Unsigned numbers take up more memory Unsigned numbers can't represent zero Unsigned numbers are slower to compute Same motivation as earlier in this lesson: unsigned is zero-or-positive only, so a signed scheme is needed to express negatives at all. It indicates the sign of the number only It stores half the magnitude It is always 0 It has no defined role In signed magnitude, the MSB is a dedicated sign flag; the remaining bits store the magnitude directly, unmodified. title: Lesson 6 · Ranges
text: Lesson 6 · Ranges A fixed n -bit representation can only hold so many distinct values (2 n of them, since each bit is independently 0 or 1). Which values those 2 n bit patterns mean depends on whether the type is unsigned or two's-complement signed — so the same bit width supports two different ranges. Type Range for n bits Range for 8 bits Unsigned [0, 2 n −1] [0, 255] Two's complement (signed) [−2 n−1 , 2 n−1 −1] [−128, 127] Both ranges hold exactly 2 n values — signed just shifts about half of them to the negative side, and the negative side gets one extra value (there's a −2 n−1 but no matching +2 n−1 ), because two's complement has only one representation of zero, not a separate +0 and −0. Multiple choice What is the range of a signed (two's complement) 8-bit integer? [0, 255] [-127, 127] [-128, 127] [-128, 128] General formula [-2 n-1 , 2 n-1 -1] with n=8 gives [-128, 127] — one more negative value than positive, since there's only one zero.

title: Lesson 6 · Binary Addition & Overflow
text: Lesson 6 · Binary Addition & Overflow Binary addition works exactly like decimal addition by hand: add column by column from the right, and when a column's sum is 2 or more, write down the low bit and carry a 1 into the next column to the left. Terminology Term Meaning Carry-in the carry bit coming into a column from the column to its right Carry-out the carry bit produced out of a column, passed to the column on its left Every column's carry-out becomes the next column's carry-in. The carry-out of the very last (most significant) column has nowhere left to go — it either gets discarded (and may signal overflow) or, in some hardware, is captured in a special flag. Worked example (unsigned, 8-bit) 0111 0101 (117) + 0010 1100 ( 44) ----------- 1010 0001 (161) Column by column from the right, tracking carries, gives 0b1010_0001 , and no carry falls off the MSB column — the true sum 161 fits within 8 unsigned bits (max 255). Unsigned overflow Detection rule (unsigned): overflow occurred exactly when the carry-out of the most-significant (last) column is 1 — the true mathematical sum needed one more bit than the type has, so that extra bit was silently dropped. Analogy: a speedometer that maxes out at 99 and wraps to 00 on the next mile doesn't show an error — it just silently wraps. Unsigned overflow in fixed-width binary works the same way: the hardware doesn't stop you, it just drops the extra carry bit and the stored value wraps around. 1111 1111 (255, the max 8-bit unsigned value) + 0000 0001 ( 1) ----------- 1 0000 0000 ← carry-out of the last column is 1: OVERFLOW 0000 0000 (stored result: 0, not 256 — wrapped around) True / False Unsigned overflow is detected when the carry-out of the most significant bit's column is 1. True False True. That extra carry bit has nowhere to go in a fixed-width unsigned number — its presence means the true sum didn't fit. 8-bit unsigned addition: 0b1111_1110 + 0b0000_0011 = ? Does it overflow? Give the stored 8-bit result as 0bXXXX_XXXX . Check 254 + 3 = 257, which needs 9 bits. The 8-bit stored result wraps to 0b0000_0001 (1) with a carry-out of 1 from the last column — overflow.

title: Lesson 6 · Two's Complement Addition, Subtraction & Overflow
text: Lesson 6 · Two's Complement Addition, Subtraction & Overflow Addition Two's complement addition uses the exact same binary addition procedure as unsigned — add column by column, carry as needed. No special-casing for sign is required; that's the whole point of two's complement (§4.4's "arithmetic wraps around correctly"). 0000 0101 ( 5) + 1111 1011 (-5) ------------ 1 0000 0000 (carry-out of last column is 1 and discarded) 0000 0000 (0) — correct! 5 + (-5) = 0 Two's complement overflow The carry-out rule from unsigned does NOT apply here. Two's complement overflow is detected differently: it happens exactly when the sign of the result doesn't make sense given the signs of the operands. Operand signs Can overflow? Overflow signature positive + positive yes result comes out negative negative + negative yes result comes out positive mixed signs (one pos, one neg) never — the true sum is always between the two operands in magnitude, so it always fits Worked example: adding two positives that overflow into a negative result, 8-bit 100 + 100 : 0110 0100 (100) + 0110 0100 (100) ----------- 1100 1000 (interpreted as signed: -56, but 100+100=200 should be +200 — overflow!) A real-world example of exactly this bug: 32-bit signed integer overflow has caused real, documented incidents where a counter that should keep climbing instead flips to a large negative number once it crosses 2 31 −1. Subtraction: negate and add Two's complement has no separate subtraction circuitry: a − b is computed as a + (−b) , where −b is b's two's complement negation (flip every bit of b , then add 1). This reuses the same adder hardware for both operations. Worked example, 8-bit 20 − 5 : 5 = 0000 0101 -5 = 1111 1010 + 1 = 1111 1011 (flip bits, add 1) 0001 0100 ( 20) + 1111 1011 ( -5) ----------- 0000 1111 ( 15) — correct! 20 - 5 = 15 Overflow detection for subtraction uses the same sign-based rule as addition, once you've rewritten it as "add the negation": check the signs of a and (−b) , not the signs of a and the original b . Multiple choice Adding a positive and a negative two's-complement number can overflow. True or false? True — it can overflow just like same-sign addition False — mixed-sign addition can never overflow False is correct. When the operands have opposite signs, the true sum's magnitude is always smaller than at least one operand's magnitude, so it always fits in the same width — only same-sign addition (pos+pos or neg+neg) can overflow. Multiple choice Two positive 8-bit two's complement numbers are added and the result appears negative. What happened? This is normal and expected A carry-out of the last column occurred, which always means overflow here Signed overflow occurred — the true sum needed more than 8 bits and the sign bit got corrupted The subtraction rule was used by mistake pos + pos should never be negative — a negative result is exactly the overflow signature for two positive operands.

title: Lesson 6 · Two's Complement in C
text: Lesson 6 · Two's Complement in C C's int (and int8_t , int16_t , etc.) are signed two's complement by default. The exact same bit pattern in memory is interpreted completely differently depending on whether the variable (or the format specifier used to print it) is signed or unsigned — the bits never change, only the interpretation does. Worked example: int8_t x = -100; uint8_t y = (uint8_t) x; // same bit pattern, reinterpreted printf("%d\\n", x); // -100 (signed interpretation of 0b1001_1100) printf("%u\\n", y); // 156 (unsigned interpretation of the SAME bits) A closely related C gotcha from the reading: printing the same variable once with %d and once with %u can print -100 and 4294967196 for what is really the identical 32-bit pattern — the bit pattern is simply interpreted differently by each format specifier (signed vs. unsigned). Casting (or choosing a different printf format specifier) never changes the stored bits — it only changes how those bits are read back as a number. ASCII reference (for context — ties casting/ interpretation to character codes) Char Dec Char Dec Char Dec '0' – '9' 48–57 'A' – 'Z' 65–90 'a' – 'z' 97–122 ' ' (space) 32 '\\n' 10 '\\0' 0 Same underlying idea: a byte's bit pattern is meaningless on its own — ASCII, signed int, and unsigned int are three different lenses for reading the identical bits. Multiple choice Why does printing a variable's bit pattern with %d vs. %u give different results? The compiler changes the stored bits based on the format specifier The bit pattern is interpreted differently — signed vs. unsigned — by each specifier This is undefined behavior with no consistent explanation %u only works for characters The bits in memory never change. %d reads them as signed two's complement; %u reads the identical bits as unsigned.

title: RD06 · Signed Binary Integers & Binary Arithmetic — Self-Check
text: RD06 · Signed Binary Integers & Binary Arithmetic — Self-Check Covers Dive into Systems §4.4–4.5 (Two's Complement, Sign/Zero Extension). Q1 Why does an MSB (most significant bit) of 1 in two's complement always mean the number is negative? By convention only, with no mathematical reason Because the MSB is always ignored in arithmetic The MSB contributes a large negative value to the total sum Because the CPU flags it as negative In two's complement's weighted-sum definition, the MSB's place value is −2 n−1 (negative), so setting it always pulls the total sum negative. Q2 How does two's complement simplify the transition between positive and negative numbers, and to/from zero? It requires separate hardware for positive and negative numbers Arithmetic naturally "wraps around" correctly It stores a separate sign bit that's checked manually It doesn't — the transition is a special case Ordinary binary addition (with carries) just works across the zero boundary and the positive/negative boundary — no special-casing needed. Q3 What is the shortcut for negating a two's complement number? Flip only the sign bit Subtract 1 from every bit Flip all bits and add one Reverse the bit order Bitwise NOT ( ~x ), then + 1 — the standard "invert and increment" negation shortcut. Q4 How does C interpret a plain int by default? As a signed two's complement integer As an unsigned integer As a one's complement integer As a floating-point value Plain int is signed two's complement unless declared unsigned . Q5 What happens when you print the same bit pattern once with %d and once with %u ? Both always print the same number The bit pattern is interpreted differently by each specifier It causes a compile error %u is invalid for integers Same bits, different lens: %d reads them as signed, %u reads them as unsigned. Q6 Why might a program print -100 and 4294967196 for what is really the same 32-bit variable's bit pattern? The variable actually holds two different values Because the bit pattern is interpreted as unsigned in the second case Integer overflow occurred between the two prints This indicates a memory corruption bug -100 as signed two's complement and 4294967196 as unsigned are the exact same 32-bit pattern, read two different ways. Q7 Why is two's complement superior to signed-magnitude representation? It uses fewer bits It can represent larger numbers It simplifies hardware design and arithmetic It avoids the need for a sign bit entirely Two's complement lets addition/subtraction hardware work identically for signed and unsigned operands, with no special sign-checking logic — signed-magnitude cannot do this. Q8 Why is bit extension necessary in C? To make numbers print faster To save memory Because arithmetic operations require operands to have the same number of bits To convert between signed and unsigned types Before combining values of different widths, the narrower one must be widened so both operands line up bit-for-bit. Q9 Which of these is an example C scenario needing bit extension? Printing a string Adding a 32-bit int and a 16-bit short Declaring a variable Comparing two floats The 16-bit short must be extended to 32 bits before it can be added to the 32-bit int . Q10 What does sign extension mean? Repeating the most significant bit to increase bit width Adding zeros to the left regardless of sign Adding zeros to the right Removing the sign bit Sign extension widens a number by repeating its MSB (sign bit) into all the new leading positions. Q11 Which bit gets repeated during sign extension? The least significant bit The most significant (sign) bit Bit 0 of the original number, always A fixed bit chosen by the compiler The current MSB (sign bit) is copied into every new leading position. Q12 How does the sign of a number stay the same after sign extension? It doesn't — sign extension can flip the sign It remains the same as the original number The sign is recalculated from scratch A separate sign flag is set Because the new leading bits copy the original sign bit, the numeric value's weighted sum — and therefore its sign — is unchanged. Q13 If zeros were wrongly prepended to a negative two's complement number instead of sign-extending, what would happen? title: HW2 · Stack Frames Deep-Dive
text: HW2 · Stack Frames Deep-Dive Reinforces Lesson 4's memory-diagram model of function calls: where frames are drawn, how the stack pointer (sp) moves, and what "returning" actually does to the diagram. The basics, reinforced Question Answer Where is a callee's frame drawn relative to the caller's? Below the caller's frame Which direction does the stack grow in our memory diagrams? From higher memory addresses toward lower memory addresses What does the stack pointer (sp) represent? The memory address marking the current end of the stack What happens to sp when a new frame is created? It moves down , toward lower memory addresses What does the return address (RA) represent? Where execution should continue after the function returns Reading a frame entry Given a memory-diagram entry like x (4): 12 : The parenthesized number ( 4 ) is the number of bytes occupied by x — not its value, not its address, and not a line number. The value after the colon ( 12 ) is the actual stored value. If main calls a function add whose return value main needs, the label used for that return-value slot in main 's frame is RV(add) — distinct from RA (the return address ) and SP (the stack pointer). What happens when a function returns Two things happen to the memory diagram when a function returns: sp moves back up (toward higher addresses, undoing the down-move that created the frame), and the returning function's old frame gets an X put through it . Nothing is erased byte-by-byte and the memory doesn't stop existing — the X just marks that the frame is no longer valid , even though its old data may still physically remain in memory until something overwrites it. What belongs in a stack frame? A function's stack frame holds its parameters , its local variables , and information about where execution should return (RA/RV) — but not every global variable in the program (globals live elsewhere, not on the stack). A #define d constant does not get its own stack slot. Given #define SIZE 5 used to declare int values[SIZE]; , SIZE itself does not receive a location in the frame, because #define is a preprocessor directive — it's textually substituted before compilation even begins, so there's no SIZE variable left to store by the time the program runs. Arrays and pointers in frames When an array like numbers is passed to a function foo(int arr[]) , the memory diagram should show a pointer in foo 's frame with an arrow drawn back to the original array in the caller's frame — the array itself is never copied into the callee's frame. Multiple choice Where should a callee's stack frame be drawn relative to its caller's? Above the caller's frame Below the caller's frame Inside the caller's frame Either above or below The callee's frame is always drawn below the caller's — the stack grows toward lower memory addresses as new calls are made. Multiple choice Why put an X through a stack frame after its function returns, rather than treating that memory as gone? The memory no longer physically exists Every byte in the frame has automatically become zero The frame is no longer valid, although its old data may still physically remain in memory The function encountered an error The X is a validity marker, not proof of erasure — the bytes can still be sitting in memory (this is exactly why using a pointer to a returned-from frame is undefined behavior: the data might look fine, or might already be overwritten). Select all that apply Which of the following may be stored in a function's stack frame? A. Parameters to the function B. Local variables C. Information about where execution should return after the function finishes D. Every global variable in the program Check A, B, and C. Globals ( D ) live in a separate region of memory, not inside any individual function's frame. Tracing frame order across calls Suppose active frames are arranged, highest address first: main, foo, bar . While bar is executing, what do the active frames look like right after bar returns to foo ? Only bar 's frame is removed — the frames left are, from highest to lowest address, main, foo . Nothing about main or foo changes; a return only ever removes the single frame that's returning. Second example — given doubleIt(int n) called from compute(int x) called from main() , while doubleIt is executing, the active frames from highest to lowest memory address are: main → compute → doubleIt — each caller's frame sits above (higher address than) the frame of the function it called. Ordering the events of a function call For int foo() { return 5; } int main() { int x = foo(); } , put these five events in execution order: (1) foo's frame is deallocated, (2) main's frame is created, (3) foo's return value is placed in RV(foo), (4) foo's frame is created, (5) sp moves back up. Check main 's frame must exist first (2) before it can call foo , whose frame is then created (4); foo computes its result and places it in RV(foo) (3) before its frame is torn down (1) and sp moves back up (5). For doubleIt(int n) called as doubleIt(4) from main , order these seven events: (1) doubleIt's return value is placed in RV(doubleIt), (2) main's stack frame is created, (3) doubleIt's stack frame is deallocated, (4) doubleIt's stack frame is created, (5) result is assigned the value 8, (6) sp moves back up after doubleIt returns, (7) the argument n receives the value 4. Check main 's frame exists first (2), then doubleIt 's frame is created (4) and its parameter n receives 4 (7); inside the body, result is computed as 8 (5) and placed in the return slot (1); only then is the frame torn down (3) and sp restored (6). For addOne(int x) called from calculate(int n) called from main as calculate(5) , order these eleven events: (1) calculate's return value is placed in RV(calculate), (2) addOne's stack frame is deallocated, (3) calculate's stack frame is created, (4) addOne's return value is placed in RV(addOne), (5) main's stack frame is created, (6) calculate's stack frame is deallocated, (7) addOne's stack frame is created, (8) addOne's local variable result is assigned 6, (9) calculate's local variable answer is assigned 6, (10) sp moves back up after addOne returns, (11) sp moves back up after calculate returns. Check Each call nests one level deeper before anything unwinds: main → calculate → addOne all get created and run to completion of addOne first (5, 3, 7, 8, 4), then addOne unwinds (2, 10) before calculate finishes its own work (9, 1) and unwinds (6, 11).

title: HW2 · Pass by Value vs. Pass by Pointer
text: HW2 · Pass by Value vs. Pass by Pointer Passing by value gives the called function a copy of the argument, stored in its own frame slot — changing the parameter can never affect the caller's original variable. Passing by pointer gives the called function a pointer that can refer back to the original variable, so writes through that pointer do affect the caller's data. Pass by value void change(int32_t x) { x = 20; } int main() { int32_t x = 10; change(x); } // main's x is still 10 — change() only modified its own copy Correct statements about pass by value: the function receives a copy of the argument's value; the parameter has its own location in the called function's stack frame; changing the parameter does not change the caller's original variable. ("Changing the parameter changes the caller's original variable" is false — that's what makes pass by value pass by value .) Arrays are effectively passed by pointer void update(int32_t arr[]) { arr[0] = 100; } int main() { int32_t values[3] = {1, 2, 3}; update(values); } // values[0] is now 100 — update() wrote through to the original array In C, an array argument decays to a pointer to its first element. So even though there's no explicit * or & in the call, update can still modify the caller's original array: the entire array is not copied, the original stays in the caller's frame, the callee can change its elements, and those changes are still visible after the callee returns. Mixing value and array parameters Given void update(int32_t x, int32_t arr[]) { x = 100; arr[0] = 100; } called as update(x, nums) where main has x = 5 and nums = {1, 2, 3} : After update returns: x = 5, nums = {100, 2, 3} — the plain int32_t x parameter is pass-by-value (caller's x untouched), while the array parameter still refers back to the caller's original nums (its first element changes). Multiple choice What does it mean to pass an argument by value? The called function receives a copy of the argument's value The called function receives the memory address of the original variable The original variable is moved into the called function's stack frame Both functions use the same variable A copy, stored in the callee's own frame slot — the caller's variable is never touched. Multiple choice What does it mean to pass a variable by pointer? The called function receives a copy of the variable's value The called function receives a pointer that can refer to the original variable The original variable is copied into the called function's stack frame The caller's stack frame is removed A pointer refers back to the original storage location, so writes through it are visible to the caller. Given void change(int32_t x){ x = 20; } int main(){ int32_t x = 10; change(x); } — what is main 's x after change returns? Check Still 10 . change 's parameter x is a separate copy in its own frame — assigning to it never reaches back into main . Given void update(int32_t arr[]){ arr[0] = 100; } called on int32_t values[3] = {1,2,3}; update(values); — what is values[0] after update returns? Check Arrays decay to a pointer when passed — arr refers to the same memory as values , so the write through arr[0] is visible in main as 100 .

title: HW2 · $PATH & Running Programs
text: HW2 · $PATH & Running Programs Whether you type an explicit path ( ./analyze ) or a bare name ( analyze ) changes how the shell decides which program actually runs. Worked scenario Current directory: /home/student/lab . Three executable files named analyze exist: /usr/local/bin/analyze , /home/student/tools/analyze , and /home/student/lab/analyze . $PATH is /usr/local/bin:/home/student/tools:/usr/bin:/bin . You type… What runs Why ./analyze /home/student/lab/analyze An explicit relative path always wins — $PATH is never consulted analyze /usr/local/bin/analyze A bare name is searched for in $PATH order; /usr/local/bin is listed first ../tools/analyze /home/student/tools/analyze Another explicit (relative) path — again, $PATH is irrelevant Any slash in what you type makes it an explicit path. The moment a command contains a / (whether ./ , ../ , or a full absolute path), the shell resolves it directly and never searches $PATH at all. Only a bare name with no slash triggers a $PATH search. Changing $PATH changes what a bare name resolves to If $PATH is changed to /home/student/tools:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin (tools now listed first ), then typing analyze now runs /home/student/tools/analyze instead — the search order changed, so the first match along the new $PATH changed too, even though nothing about the files themselves moved. You're in /home/student/lab with an executable at that same path; typing ./analyze runs which absolute path? True / False Typing a bare command name with no slash triggers a search through $PATH , in order, for the first matching executable. True False True. The shell walks the colon-separated directories in $PATH left to right and runs the first executable match it finds.

Goal Command Key idea Every line containing Alice grep "Alice" students.txt Plain substring match — no metacharacters needed Every line that starts with A grep "^A" students.txt ^ anchors to the start of the line Every line that ends with a grep "a$" students.txt $ anchors to the end of the line Lines starting with A and ending with a , anything between grep "^A.*a$" students.txt .* = any number of any character Lines containing Bob followed by zero or more b characters grep "Bobb*" students.txt * repeats the single character right before it (here, the second b ) zero or more times Lines containing student followed by exactly one character grep "student." students.txt Unescaped . = exactly one any character Lines containing any digit 0–9 grep "[0-9]" students.txt [0-9] is a character-class range Lines beginning with A, B, or C grep "^[ABC]" students.txt Combine an anchor with a character class Lines ending with a digit grep "[0-9]$" students.txt Combine a character class with the end anchor Lines containing at least one lowercase vowel grep "[aeiou]" students.txt Character classes don't need ranges — an explicit list works too Bobb* , not Bob* . title: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Assembling
text: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Assembling Computers cannot understand Python, Java, or C. They understand machine code : binary instructions — strings of 1s and 0s — that tell the processor what operations to perform. Everything else is a translation layer built to spare humans from writing that. How we got from bits to C Era What you wrote What made it possible Before the 1950s Machine code , entered by switches, punch cards, or paper tape nothing — you were the translator Early 1950s Assembly language — human-readable mnemonics like add x8, x9, x10 Assemblers , programs that translate assembly into machine code Late 1950s High-level languages that abstract away the hardware and focus on logic and algorithms Compilers Machines still cannot read assembly — only machine code. The assembler exists precisely to automate that conversion, and it is what let programmers write and debug far more efficiently. The three languages the slides name Year Language Why it mattered 1957 FORTRAN (FORmula TRANslation) First widely adopted high-level language; built by IBM for scientific and engineering calculations 1958 LISP (LISt Processor) Pioneered functional programming and symbolic processing 1959 COBOL (COmmon Business-Oriented Language) Business applications; emphasized readability and portability; became the enterprise/financial standard Low-level vs high-level Machine code Assembly (low-level) C (high-level) Looks like 0b0000000010100100... add x8, x9, x10 return num * num; Readable by the machine humans, with effort humans, easily Tied to a specific processor yes yes no C is a compiled high-level language. To execute it, the program is first translated into assembly by a compiler , then the assembler translates that assembly into machine code . Two translations, two different tools. Interpreted languages like Python are executed differently — no separate compile-then-run step producing a machine-code file. Multiple choice What does a compiler translate, and into what? Assembly language into machine code A high-level language into assembly language Machine code into a high-level language Source code directly into output on the screen Compiler: high-level → assembly . Option 0 is the assembler . Two distinct programs, run one after the other — gcc just hides the seam by doing both. Multiple choice Why do assemblers exist? Because machines cannot read machine code Because C is faster than assembly Because machines cannot read assembly language — something has to convert it to machine code Because assembly is a high-level language Machines read only machine code. Assembly is for humans; the assembler automates the conversion. Option 0 has it exactly backwards.

title: Lesson 2 · Your First C Program
text: Lesson 2 · Your First C Program #include <stdio.h> int main () { printf ( "Hello, world!\\n" ); return 0 ; } Line Why it is there #include <stdio.h> printf is a standard library function. C does not automatically include any standard library functions — to use printf you must explicitly include stdio.h . int main() All C programs begin executing at main . It returns an int — the program's exit status . return 0; A successful execution returns 0 . An abnormal execution returns a non-zero value. Note the direction of that convention: 0 means success , which is the opposite of the usual "0 is false" intuition. Non-zero is how a program reports which thing went wrong. The C Standard Library A collection of pre-written functions for common tasks: input/output, string manipulation, mathematical operations, memory management. The functions are grouped into header files . A header file contains the declarations of the functions, macros, and types you can use. Term Meaning Function declaration the function's name, return type, and parameters Function definition the body of the function The header gives you the declaration so the compiler knows how to call the function; the definition lives in the compiled library. Header file Purpose Example functions <stdio.h> Input/output printf, getchar, putchar, fopen <stdlib.h> General utilities malloc, free, exit, atoi, rand <string.h> String manipulation strlen, strcpy, strcat, strcmp <math.h> Mathematical operations sqrt, pow, sin, cos, tan, exp <time.h> Date and time time, clock, localtime, gmtime Multiple choice You call strlen but forget #include <string.h> . Why is that a problem? The function does not exist without the include C automatically includes it anyway, so it is fine C does not automatically include standard library functions — without the header the compiler has no declaration for strlen Header files are optional in C The function's definition exists in the library either way, but the compiler needs the declaration from the header to know its return type and parameters. The slides state it plainly: "C does not automatically include any standard library functions." Multiple choice What does the value returned by main represent? The number of lines the program printed The program's exit status — 0 for success, non-zero for abnormal The amount of memory used Nothing; it is ignored The exit status . This is how the shell (and tools like make ) find out whether your program succeeded.

title: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Running with gcc
text: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Running with gcc Write your program. Save it with a .c extension — say hello.c . Open a terminal and cd to the directory where the program lives. Compile and assemble: gcc hello.c Run it: ./a.out gcc invokes the G NU C C ompiler. It converts your human-readable C code into a machine-readable executable file . Command Executable produced gcc hello.c a.out (the default) gcc hello.c -o hello hello gcc -o hello hello.c hello gcc hello.c -o hi hi The -o rule. The executable name must immediately follow -o . Everything else about the ordering is flexible — notice rows 2 and 3 produce the same result with -o hello on either side of the source file. What you cannot do is separate -o from its argument. Why ./ ? . means the current directory (straight from Lesson 1), so ./a.out says "run the a.out that is right here." The ./ is required because the current directory is not in your PATH — the list of directories the shell searches for commands. Type a bare a.out and the shell searches PATH , does not find it, and reports "command not found," even though the file is sitting right in front of you. This is a deliberate security decision: if . were on the PATH, dropping a malicious file named ls into a directory would hijack the real ls . If you named the executable hello , run it with ./hello . In-class problem — multiple select Which of these sets of commands compile, assemble, and execute the program in my_program.c ? Tick every one that works. A. gcc my_program.c then ./my_program.c B. gcc my_program.c -o my_program then ./a.out C. gcc my_program.c -o my_prog then ./my_prog D. gcc my_program.c then ./a.out E. gcc my_program.c -o my_program then ./my_program.c Check C and D. The single idea being tested: you run the executable, never the .c source file. A and E both try to execute my_program.c — that is source code, not a program. B renames the executable to my_program with -o , so a.out was never created; ./a.out fails. D uses the default name a.out and runs a.out . C names it my_prog and runs my_prog . Both are consistent.

title: Lesson 2 · Variables and Types
text: Lesson 2 · Variables and Types Property Meaning Scope Where in a program you can use a variable Lifetime When the variable exists in memory Type The range of values the variable can represent, and how the value will be interpreted That second half of "type" is the one worth underlining. A type does not only bound the values — it decides what the bits mean . The same byte is 65 or 'A' depending on how you read it, which is the entire subject of the next tab. C numeric types Type Usual size Values stored Declaration char 1 byte integers char x; short 2 bytes signed integers short x; int 4 bytes signed integers int x; long 4 or 8 bytes signed integers long x; long long 8 bytes signed integers long long x; float 4 bytes signed real numbers float x; double 8 bytes signed real numbers double x; 8 bits = 1 byte. So an int is 32 bits, and a char is 8. "Usual" is doing real work in that table. The exact number of bytes for each C type might vary from one architecture to the next — which is why long is listed as "4 or 8." Never hard-code a size you did not measure. Measuring with sizeof The sizeof operator takes the name of a type and evaluates to the number of bytes used to store it. printf ( "number of bytes in an int: %lu\\n" , sizeof ( int )); printf ( "number of bytes in a short: %lu\\n" , sizeof ( short )); sizeof evaluates to an unsigned long , so print it with %lu — not %d . This is a real compiler warning you will hit. Multiple choice Which placeholder should you use to print sizeof(int) ? %d %s %lu %c sizeof evaluates to an unsigned long , so %lu . Multiple choice How many bits are in a typical int ? 4 32 8 64 4 bytes × 8 bits per byte = 32 bits . The "4" in the table is bytes, not bits — read that column carefully.

title: Lesson 2 · printf
text: Lesson 2 · printf C's printf is very similar to Java's System.out.printf : the caller supplies a format string to print. The format string contains formatting specifiers — special characters that print tabs ( \\t ) or newlines ( \\n ), and placeholders for values. A placeholder is % followed by a type-specifier letter , and for each placeholder, printf expects an additional argument . Placeholders Placeholder Used for Example Output %d Signed integer printf("%d", 25); 25 %u Unsigned integer printf("%u", 25); 25 %f Floating-point number printf("%f", 3.14); 3.14 %c Single character printf("%c", 'A'); A %s String printf("%s", "Hello"); Hello %lu Unsigned long (e.g. sizeof ) printf("%lu", sizeof(int)); 4 Special characters (escape sequences) A special character has a specific meaning or function in the language rather than simply representing ordinary text. In C, escape sequences use a backslash ( \\ ) to represent them — which lets you include characters that are difficult to type or represent directly. Sequence Name Meaning Example \\n Newline Moves to the next line "Hello\\nWorld" \\t Tab Inserts a horizontal tab "Name:\\tJohn" \\\\ Backslash Prints a \\ "C:\\\\Users" \\" Double quote Prints a " inside a string "He said \\"Hello\\"" \\0 Null character Marks the end of a C string "Hello\\0" %% Percent sign Prints a % when using printf printf("50%%"); Two different escape characters doing two different jobs. \\ introduces a special character; % introduces a placeholder. That is why a literal percent sign is %% and not \\% — it is escaping within printf's own notation, not C's. Match each specifier %d — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %c — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %s — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign \\n — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign \\t — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %% — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign Check

title: Lesson 2 · Characters and ASCII
text: Lesson 2 · Characters and ASCII ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange . It is a code that lets computers represent text using numbers. The C char type stores a numeric value — but it is most often used to hold the value of an ASCII character. Values worth memorizing Character ASCII value 'A' 65 'B' 66 'a' 97 '0' 48 space 32 '!' 33 Learn 65, 97, 48 and the rest follow: letters and digits run consecutively, and lowercase is exactly 32 above uppercase. With 8 bits An unsigned char holds the values [0, 2 8 −1] = [0, 255] . That is comfortably more than enough for the ASCII set. Bits are just bits. To give bits meaning you must assign them a representation , which defines how they correspond to meaningful information. Take the value 0b0100 0001 : • as a decimal integer it reads as 65 • as an ASCII character it reads as 'A' Nothing about the bits changed. Only the interpretation did. %c vs %d — the same value, two readings printf ( "%c\\n" , 'A' ); // A printf ( "%d\\n" , 'A' ); // 65 Give it a character and ask for a number: you get the ASCII code. printf ( "%c\\n" , 67 ); // C printf ( "%d\\n" , 87 ); // 87 Give it a number and ask for a character: you get the character with that ASCII encoding. The placeholder chooses the interpretation. The value being passed is a number either way. Character arithmetic Because a char is a number, you can do arithmetic with characters. printf ( "%d\\n" , 'a' - 'C' ); The ASCII value of 'C' is 67 and of 'a' is 97, so this prints 30 . The genuinely useful version of this trick is the constant 'a' - 'A' = 32 , the gap between lowercase and uppercase. Subtract it from a lowercase letter and you get the uppercase one — which is exactly how the in-class echo program works. Why we are learning this The slides make the point explicitly: ASCII is not specific to C. Computers ultimately represent all data using binary, including letters, digits, and symbols. Regardless of the language you use, characters must be represented numerically so the computer can store and process them. Learning ASCII is how you internalize the relationship between characters and their numeric representations — the same "bits are just bits" idea that runs through the entire course.

title: Lesson 2 · getchar , putchar , and EOF
text: Lesson 2 · getchar , putchar , and EOF Function What it does getchar() Reads one character from the input (a keyboard or a file) and returns it as an integer putchar(c) Takes the character stored in c and prints it to the output Both live in <stdio.h> , so you need that include. #include <stdio.h> int main () { int my_char = getchar (); printf ( "The user entered: %c\\n" , my_char); } EOF, and why getchar returns an int EOF stands for End of File . It is a special value returned by getchar() when there is no more input to read. EOF is the reason getchar() returns an int instead of a char . EOF must be distinguishable from any valid character. In the ASCII character set all valid characters are encoded as integers from 0 to 255 ; if EOF were encoded as a char it could collide with a real character value. The slides give the concrete case: if EOF were represented as 255 on a system where char is unsigned, it would conflict with the ASCII value for the ÿ character. An int is wider than a char , so there is room for a value outside 0–255 that no real character can ever equal. You signal EOF manually with Ctrl + D on Linux/macOS, or Ctrl + Z on Windows. The echo loop, two ways This reads characters until EOF and prints each one — it copies input to output, one character at a time. Explicit int main () { int c = getchar (); while (c != EOF) { putchar (c); c = getchar (); } } Concise (the idiom) int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { putchar (c); } } The right-hand version reads inside the condition: first c gets the next character, then the while checks whether that character is EOF. The inner parentheses around (c = getchar()) are required — without them, precedence would compare getchar() to EOF first and assign the resulting 0 or 1 to c . Multiple choice Why does getchar() return an int rather than a char ? Because int is faster on modern hardware Because characters can be larger than one byte So EOF can be a value distinguishable from every valid character (0–255) Because putchar requires an int EOF has to be a value that no real character can equal . A char has no spare values left; an int does. True / False In while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) , the inner parentheses are optional style. True False They are required . != binds tighter than = , so c = getchar() != EOF would compare first and then assign the comparison result (0 or 1) into c — the loop would run, but c would never hold a character.

title: Lesson 3 · Arrays and #define
text: Lesson 3 · Arrays and #define Arrays in C are a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory holding elements of the same type. Unlike Java, a C array does not know its own size — there is no .length . The programmer must track the size separately, often with a #define d constant. Digit-counting program A classic example: read characters until EOF, and count how many times each digit '0'–'9' appears. #include <stdio.h> #define NUM_DIGITS 10 int main () { int ndigit[NUM_DIGITS] = { 0 }; int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { if (c >= '0' && c <= '9' ) { ++ndigit[c - '0' ]; } } for ( int i = 0 ; i < NUM_DIGITS; i++) { printf ( "digit %d: %d\\n" , i, ndigit[i]); } } int ndigit[NUM_DIGITS] = {0}; declares an array of 10 ints and initializes every element to 0 (a partial brace initializer zero-fills the rest). Why ++ndigit[c - '0'] and not the tempting alternatives Expression What it actually does Verdict ++ndigit[c - '0']; c is a character code (e.g. '5' = 53). Subtracting '0' (48) converts it to the numeric digit value 5, a valid index 0–9. Correct ndigit[c]++; Uses the raw character code as the index . c for '5' is 53 — miles past the array's 10 slots. Wrong — out-of-bounds access ndigit['c'-'0']++; This is the literal letter 'c' (99) minus '0' (48) = a fixed constant, 51 . It never reads the loop variable at all. Wrong — nonsense fixed index, and still out of bounds The bug is easy to miss visually. ndigit[c] and ndigit['c'-'0'] both look like they involve the character we just read, but neither one does what ndigit[c - '0'] does: take the variable c 's ASCII code and subtract the code for '0' to land on a small index. Multiple choice Given char c = '7'; , what does c - '0' evaluate to? 7 55 48 A compiler error — you cannot subtract characters '7' is ASCII 55, '0' is ASCII 48. 55 − 48 = 7 — the numeric value of the digit character. This is exactly the trick used to convert a digit character to its value. True / False ndigit[c]++; is a safe, equivalent replacement for ++ndigit[c - '0']; when c holds a digit character. True False False. c is the raw ASCII code (e.g. 53 for '5' ), which is far larger than the array's 10 elements — an out-of-bounds write. #define : preprocessor text substitution #define NAME value is a preprocessor directive — a pure find-and-replace performed on the source text before compilation even starts . It is not a variable. #define NUM_DIGITS 10 const int num_digits = 10; Memory allocated None — it never exists at runtime Yes, a real memory location Type checking None — it is just swapped-in text Yes, it has a declared type When it happens Preprocessing, before compiling Compile time / runtime What the compiler sees Every occurrence of NUM_DIGITS literally replaced by 10 A named, typed variable Think of #define as your editor's "find and replace," run once, automatically, on the whole file before the compiler ever looks at it. No memory, no type, no runtime existence — it is gone by the time the compiler starts working. The four-stage build process Stage Tool Job 1. Preprocessor cpp Handles #include (pastes in header contents) and #define (text substitution). Produces expanded source text. 2. Compiler cc1 Translates the expanded C source into assembly language for the target processor. 3. Assembler as Translates assembly into object code (machine code) — a .o file. 4. Linker ld Combines your object file(s) with library object code (e.g. the implementation of printf ) into one final executable . gcc hello.c runs all four stages for you in one command, which is why nothing visibly "stops" between them. Multiple choice Which stage expands #define macros and #include directives? The compiler The preprocessor The assembler The linker The preprocessor runs first and handles all lines starting with # — pure text manipulation before any real compiling happens. Multiple choice Which stage combines your object file with the library code for functions like printf to produce the final executable? The preprocessor The compiler The assembler The linker The linker is the last stage — it stitches together every object file (yours and the standard library's) into one runnable program. C arrays vs Java arrays C array Java array Knows its own size? No — no .length Yes — arr.length Tracking size Programmer's responsibility (a separate size parameter, or a #define d constant) Built in to the array object Bounds checking None — out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior Runtime ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException If you write a C function that takes an array, you almost always need to pass its size too — the array itself carries no such information. Select all that apply Which statements about C arrays are true? A. A C array does not know its own length at runtime. B. Accessing an index past the end of a C array raises a runtime exception, just like Java. C. Programmers commonly use #define to name an array's size. D. ndigit[9] is out of bounds for int ndigit[NUM_DIGITS] when NUM_DIGITS is 10. Check A and C. C has no bounds checking (B is false — out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior, not a clean exception). D is false too: valid indices for a 10-element array are 0–9, so ndigit[9] is the last valid element, not out of bounds.

title: Lesson 3 · I/O Redirection
text: Lesson 3 · I/O Redirection Every running program has three standard streams, each identified by a small integer called a file descriptor : File descriptor Stream Default destination 0 stdin the keyboard 1 stdout the terminal 2 stderr the terminal stdout and stderr both print to the terminal by default, which is why you normally cannot tell them apart — until you redirect one of them. Redirection operators Syntax Effect cmd < input.txt Redirects stdin — the program reads from input.txt instead of the keyboard. cmd > output.txt Redirects stdout to output.txt , overwriting it if it exists. cmd >> output.txt Redirects stdout to output.txt , appending to the end instead of overwriting. cmd 2> errors.txt Redirects stderr only, to errors.txt . cmd > out.txt 2> err.txt Sends stdout and stderr to two separate files. > overwrites, >> appends. This is one of the most common mistakes in the course — running the same command twice with > destroys the first run's output. Demo programs readstdin.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { /* process c */ } } Reads from stdin (fd 0) via getchar() in a loop until EOF . writestdout.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { putchar ( 'x' ); } putchar() always writes to stdout (fd 1) — there is no way to redirect it to stderr by changing arguments. writestderr.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { fputc ( 'x' , stderr); /* or: fprintf(stderr, "x"); */ } Key point: putchar() can only ever write to stdout . To write to stderr , you must use a different function — fputc(ch, stderr) or fprintf(stderr, ...) — that takes the stream explicitly. Multiple choice You want a character written to stderr instead of stdout. Which function should you use? putchar(ch) printf("%c", ch) fputc(ch, stderr) There is no way to write to stderr in C putchar and plain printf are hard-wired to stdout . fputc(ch, stderr) (or fprintf(stderr, ...) ) explicitly names the stream. True / False cmd > output.txt appends to output.txt if the file already exists. True False False. A single > overwrites (truncates) the file. Use >> to append. Walkthrough: ./program < input.txt > output.txt 2> error.txt Suppose program reads numbers from stdin, prints valid results to stdout, and prints an error message to stderr for any invalid input line. Stream Where it goes stdin (fd 0) read from input.txt , not the keyboard stdout (fd 1) written to output.txt stderr (fd 2) written to error.txt What appears on the terminal nothing — both output streams were redirected to files Multiple choice Given ./program < input.txt > output.txt 2> error.txt , what shows up on the terminal while it runs? Only the error messages Nothing — both stdout and stderr were redirected to files Only the normal output Everything, because redirection doesn't affect the terminal Both 1 (stdout) and 2 (stderr) point at files here, so the terminal shows nothing from the program itself. Multiple choice Where do the program's error messages end up in that same command? output.txt the terminal error.txt input.txt 2> error.txt sends stderr specifically to error.txt , separate from stdout's output.txt .

title: Lesson 3 · Pipes
text: Lesson 3 · Pipes command1 | command2 connects command1's stdout directly to command2's stdin — no intermediate file is ever written to disk. The | character is called a pipe . Demo: producer and consumer producer.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { printf ( "apple\\n" ); printf ( "banana\\n" ); printf ( "cherry\\n" ); } Prints three lines to stdout, one fruit per line. consumer.c int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { if (c== 'a' ||c== 'e' ||c== 'i' || c== 'o' ||c== 'u' ) putchar ( '-' ); else putchar (c); } } Reads stdin character by character and replaces each vowel with - . producer | consumer feeds producer's stdout straight into consumer's stdin: Input line (from producer) Output line (from consumer) apple -ppl- banana b-n-n- cherry ch-rry Match the input line to its piped output apple — choose — -ppl- b-n-n- ch-rry banana — choose — -ppl- b-n-n- ch-rry cherry — choose — -ppl- b-n-n- ch-rry Check Each vowel (a, e, i, o, u) becomes - ; every other character, including newlines, passes through unchanged. Chaining pipes Pipes chain: producer | consumer | wc -c feeds consumer's output into wc . Command Counts wc -c characters (bytes) wc -l lines wc -w words Multiple choice What does producer | consumer | wc -l print? The total number of characters printed by consumer The number of vowels replaced The number of lines consumer produced — 3, one per fruit Nothing; you cannot chain more than one pipe Pipes chain freely. wc -l counts lines of its stdin, which here is consumer's output — 3 lines, one per fruit. True / False A pipe connects one program's stdout directly to the next program's stdin, without writing an intermediate file. True False True. That's the whole point of | — no temp file, no disk I/O in between.

title: Lesson 3 · Strings
text: Lesson 3 · Strings C has no built-in string type. A C string is just a char array terminated by the null character '\\0' . Everything that works with strings ( printf("%s", ...) , strlen , ...) relies on finding that terminator. Literal initializers: quotes matter char str1[] = "hello" ; A double-quoted string literal automatically gets a '\\0' appended. str1 is 6 bytes: h e l l o \\0 . Valid C string. char str2[] = { 'h' , 'e' , 'l' , 'l' , 'o' }; A char-array initializer list does NOT add a terminator. str2 is only 5 bytes with no '\\0' — not a valid C string . Passing it to printf("%s",...) or strlen is undefined behavior. This is a real bug pattern, not a pedantic detail. {'h','e','l','l','o'} looks like it should behave like "hello" . It does not — there is no null terminator, so any function that scans for one will read past the end of the array into whatever memory happens to follow. strlen() vs sizeof() strlen(s) sizeof(s) What it measures characters up to (not including) the first '\\0' the array's total allocated byte capacity Needs <string.h> ? Yes No — it's a compile-time operator, not a function char str3[ 10 ] = "hi" ; printf ( "%lu\\n" , sizeof (str3)); // 10 — the array's declared capacity printf ( "%lu\\n" , strlen (str3)); // 2 — chars before the first '\\0' These two numbers can differ a lot, and mixing them up is a common bug (e.g. looping sizeof times over data that's really only strlen long). An early null terminator char str4[] = { 'h' , 'i' , '\\0' , 'X' , 'Y' , 'Z' , '\\0' }; printf ( "%lu\\n" , strlen (str4)); // 2 printf ( "%lu\\n" , sizeof (str4)); // 7 strlen stops at the first '\\0' it finds — giving 2 — even though the array physically holds 7 bytes and more data ("XYZ") sits after that first terminator. strlen has no way to know that data is there. Fill in the blank char a[] = {'h','i','\\0','X','Y','Z','\\0'}; — what does strlen(a) return? Check strlen stops counting at the first '\\0' , which is at index 2. It has no visibility into what comes after. Fill in the blank Same array — what does sizeof(a) return (its total byte capacity)? Check sizeof counts every element of the array, regardless of any '\\0' inside it — all 7 bytes. Multiple choice char bad[] = {'h','e','l','l','o'}; Why is this NOT a valid C string? title: Lesson 4 · Function Stack Frames
text: Lesson 4 · Function Stack Frames Every time a function is called, the program allocates a chunk of memory for it on the call stack called a stack frame . That frame holds everything the function needs to run and to hand control back when it's done. What's inside a stack frame Field Purpose Return Address (RA) The address in the caller to resume execution at once the callee returns. Arguments The parameter values passed in by the caller. Local Variables Variables declared inside the function's own body. Caller — the function making the call. Callee — the function being called. Every call has exactly one of each. The stack pointer The stack pointer ( sp ) always points at the top of the stack — the edge of the most recently allocated frame. Event What happens to sp A function is called A new frame is pushed : sp moves to make room for it (grows the stack). A function returns The top frame is popped /deallocated: sp moves back, and that frame's memory is considered dead (conceptually "X-ed out" — its contents are no longer valid, even though the bytes may still physically sit in memory until overwritten). The stack grows with every call and shrinks with every return — a strict last-in-first-out order. The most recently called, not-yet-returned function's frame is always the one on top. Multiple choice What does a stack frame's Return Address (RA) store? The value the function will return The address in the caller to resume execution at once this function returns The address of the function's first local variable The size of the stack frame The RA is how the CPU knows where to go back to in the caller — not the function's own return value. Multiple choice When a function returns, what happens to its stack frame? It is popped/deallocated, and sp moves back down It stays on the stack forever It moves to the heap sp moves further up to make more room for it Returning pops the frame: sp moves back to where it was before the call, freeing that space for the next call. True / False The stack pointer sp always points at the bottom (oldest frame) of the stack. True False False. sp points at the top — the most recently pushed frame.

title: Lesson 4 · Call-Chain Walkthrough
text: Lesson 4 · Call-Chain Walkthrough Trace a chain of calls: main calls A , A calls B , B calls C . Watch the stack grow with each call, and unwind on each return. void C () { /* does work, returns */ } void B () { C (); } void A () { B (); } int main () { A (); } Step Call/Return Stack (top → bottom) 1 main starts main 2 main calls A A · main 3 A calls B B · A · main 4 B calls C C · B · A · main 5 C returns (frame popped) B · A · main 6 B returns (frame popped) A · main 7 A returns (frame popped) main 8 main returns (empty) Each call pushes a new frame on top; each return pops exactly one frame — the one on top, which is always the most recently called, not-yet-finished function. This is why the RA in each frame matters: when C returns, the CPU jumps to the RA stored in C 's frame, which points back into B . Multiple choice In the chain main → A → B → C , at the moment C is executing, how many stack frames exist? 1 2 4 0 One frame for each function still "in progress": main , A , B , and C itself — 4 total. Multiple choice When C returns, whose frame does the CPU resume executing in? B 's — the function that called C main 's A 's C 's own frame, restarted A return always goes back to the immediate caller — the RA stored in C 's own frame points into B , not further up the chain. True / False Stack frames are deallocated in the reverse order they were created (last pushed, first popped). True False True — the call stack is strictly LIFO (last-in, first-out).

text: Lesson 4 · Fixed-Size Integer Types Plain int 's size can vary across compilers and architectures. <stdint.h> defines types whose byte width is guaranteed , which makes stack-frame byte-arithmetic (and this lecture's diagrams) predictable and portable. Type Bit width Byte width Typical use int8_t 8 bits 1 byte small counters, byte-sized flags, raw byte data int16_t 16 bits 2 bytes compact values with a known small range (e.g. audio samples) int32_t 32 bits 4 bytes general-purpose integers — matches a typical int int64_t 64 bits 8 bytes large counts, memory addresses/offsets, pointers-worth of data Why not just use int ? Because int 's size "might vary from one architecture to the next" — exactly the same caveat from Lesson 2's numeric-types table. In stack-frame diagrams we need to say precisely "this field is 4 bytes" and have that be true everywhere, so the lecture uses int32_t etc. instead of int / short / long .
